question: The EU is increasingly recognising that access to key raw materials is a strategic economic and geopolitical priority, in accordance with the EU strategy on critical raw materials and the proposed European Critical Raw Materials Act.

Currently, the EU significantly depends on imports of critical raw materials – such as rare earth elements, lithium, cobalt, graphite and magnesium – from third countries, particularly from the People’s Republic of China, which controls 60–90 % of the global processing of some of these materials.
This structural dependence threatens the security of supply chains in sectors such as e-mobility, renewables, the defence industry and advanced digital technologies.

Despite announcements on diversifying supply, accelerating investments in extraction and recycling, and forging strategic partnerships with third countries, actions so far have been limited and fragmented, and have not created sufficient independence from China’s domination of the sector. 1.
What specific steps will the Commission take to accelerate the exploitation of critical raw material deposits in EU Member States such as Poland, Finland, Sweden and Spain?
Is the Commission planning to create derogation mechanisms to accelerate environmental and administrative procedures that are currently blocking investments in raw material extraction in the EU?
Is the Commission considering the mandatory introduction of an EU-wide critical raw materials reserve, like those already in place for gas and crude oil?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.12.2025) The European Critical Raw Materials Act1 includes several provisions to increase the exploitation of critical raw materials within the EU. Member States have prepared national exploration programmes that will increase the available information on critical raw materials deposits.

Additionally, selected strategic projects across the EU (two in Poland, three in Sweden, six in Finland and seven in Spain)2 benefit from streamlined and predictable permitting procedures and support in gaining access to finance.

The Commission, together with Member States, are working for the effective implementation of the provisions related to streamlining the permit-granting process of strategic raw materials projects while maintaining the relevant environmental standards3.
The stockpiling sub-group of the EU Critical Raw Materials Board, formed by the Commission and the Member States, is working on the reporting and coordination of stocks of strategic raw materials4.

This work will feed into the European Critical Raw Materials Centre, announced for 2026, which will focus on the joint purchasing of raw materials, coordination of strategic stockpiles, supply chain monitoring and the design of financial products to invest in upstream supply in the EU and third countries5.

On 25 October 2025, the Commission President announced the upcoming RESourceEU plan, with the aim of stepping up the efforts and accelerating the achievement of EU critical raw material objectives6. It will focus on diversification, joint purchasing, stockpiling, boosting investment in strategic projects, reinforcing the EU circular economy7 and the recycling of critical raw materials.
